title: Advanced relative clauses
tagline: Front the preposition, count the group, or drop the finite verb — three ways to sound more precise.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (preposition + whom/which, quantifier + of which)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (whereby, whom, whose, whichever)
Writing Part 1 — essay: formal register and precise reference
Writing Part 2 — reports and proposals: whereby, of which, non-finite relatives
why: Advanced relative clauses let a C1 writer be exact about how two ideas connect — not just who did what, but the precise relationship: a preposition fronted before whom or which, the means by which something happens (whereby), or a quantity already mentioned (ten of whom). C1 Advanced tests the fronted-preposition pattern directly in Use of English, and a report or proposal in the Writing paper reads noticeably more professional once repetition is replaced by a single, well-built relative clause.

branches.label: Preposition + whom/which (formal)
items: the person to whom I spoke
the reason for which she resigned
the school in which she studied

branches.label: whereby / wherein
items: a system whereby students choose their own topics
a clause wherein the terms are defined

branches.label: Quantifier + of which/whom
items: ten students, three of whom failed
two essays, neither of which was finished
a list, all of which I checked

rows.label: Example

diagrams.title: Reducing a relative clause to the infinitive

before.text: Liam was the first student who finished the marathon.

after.text: Liam was the first student to finish the marathon.

steps: This works after superlatives and words like 'the first / the last / the only'.
Drop the relative pronoun and the auxiliary or modal.
Change the verb to the to-infinitive: to finish.

head: Structure
Use
Example
rows: preposition + whom (people)
formal, a person as the object of a preposition
The colleague with whom I share an office is from Arequipa.
preposition + which (things)
formal, a thing as the object of a preposition
The method by which the data was collected is described in Appendix 2.
whereby
= by which / through which, for a system or process
The school introduced a scheme whereby senior students mentor younger ones.
quantifier + of which/whom
refers back to a whole group already mentioned
We interviewed forty candidates, five of whom withdrew before the final round.
whose / of which (things)
possession with things; whose sounds the most natural
The museum, whose collection dates back to colonial times, reopens in March.
whatever / whichever / whoever
an open category: any thing / option / person
Whichever path you take, the summit is at least three hours away.
the first/only/superlative + to-infinitive
reduces a relative clause after ordinals and superlatives
Nadia was the only student to submit her project early.
which (referring to a whole clause)
a formal comment on the entire idea just stated
The trains were cancelled, which meant we missed the connection.

use.point: Preposition + whom/which for a precise, formal link

examples.text: The professor to whom I sent my application never replied.
This is the argument on which the whole essay depends.
The village from which her grandmother came no longer appears on modern maps.

use.point: whereby and wherein for systems and processes

examples.text: The council has adopted a policy whereby every classroom recycles its own paper.
The report contains a section wherein the methodology is explained in detail.
examples.note: wherein = in which; very formal, close to legal register

use.point: Quantifier + of which/whom, and whose/of which for things

examples.text: The committee reviewed sixty applications, ten of which were rejected immediately.
Cusco has hundreds of colonial buildings, many of which are now hotels.
The theory, the basic principles of which remain unchanged, was first published in 1905.
examples.note: a long, very formal alternative to whose for abstract things

examples.text: Mateo was the last person to leave the lab that evening.
Whoever designed this exam clearly enjoyed making it difficult.
examples.note: whoever = the person who, an open reference

examples.text: Take whichever seat is free; it doesn't matter which row.
examples.note: whichever = any one of a limited set

watch_out.wrong: The teacher who I spoke to whom was very helpful.
watch_out.right: The teacher to whom I spoke was very helpful.
watch_out.why: Don't combine a fronted preposition with a stranded one — choose a single pattern.

watch_out.wrong: The system which whereby students vote was introduced last year.
watch_out.right: The system whereby students vote was introduced last year.
watch_out.why: Whereby already means 'by which'; it replaces which + preposition, it doesn't add to it.

watch_out.wrong: We tested thirty samples, which five failed.
watch_out.right: We tested thirty samples, five of which failed.
watch_out.why: After a quantity, use 'number/quantifier + of which/whom', not 'which' alone.

watch_out.wrong: The device to who I complained is being replaced.
watch_out.right: The device to which I complained is being replaced.
watch_out.why: Whom is only for people; things need which after a preposition.

watch_out.wrong: Nadia was the first who arrived to the meeting.
watch_out.right: Nadia was the first to arrive at the meeting.
watch_out.why: After 'the first/last/only' and superlatives, the non-finite to-infinitive relative is usually preferred over a finite clause.

watch_out.wrong: The bus was late, that annoyed everyone.
watch_out.right: The bus was late, which annoyed everyone.
watch_out.why: Only which — never that — can refer back to a whole previous clause.

dialogue.title: Drafting the council proposal
dialogue.context: Miss Vega reviews the formal proposal that Sofia, Liam and Mateo are writing for the school council, checking that the relative clauses sound appropriately formal.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Remember, this document goes to the council, so keep the register formal. Read me your opening sentence.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: 'We propose a scheme whereby every class manages its own recycling point.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good use of whereby — that's exactly the register we want.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: What about this: 'The teacher to who I first mentioned the idea was Mr Ramos.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Almost — whom is for people. Try again.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: 'The teacher to whom I first mentioned the idea was Mr Ramos.'

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I've written: 'We surveyed eighty students, thirty of whom said they already separate their rubbish at home.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's a strong sentence — quantifier plus 'of whom' is very natural in a report like this.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And for the conclusion: 'The pilot programme, the results of which will be published in July, starts next month.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Excellent. One more thing — can anyone make 'Nadia is the student who suggested the idea first' sound more formal?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: 'Nadia was the student to suggest the idea first.'

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Whoever reads this proposal will be impressed. Let's finish the last paragraph.

items.sentence: The teacher ___ I owe my interest in astronomy has just retired.
The bridge ___ the two towns are connected was rebuilt after the earthquake.
items.why: 'by which' refers to a thing — the bridge is the means of connection

items.sentence: The council introduced a new timetable ___ students choose four optional subjects.
items.why: whereby = by which, used for a system or process

items.sentence: We shortlisted twelve candidates, ___ withdrew before the interview.
items.why: quantifier + of whom refers back to people already mentioned

items.sentence: Sofia was the only student ___ every question correctly.
items.why: after 'the only', the non-finite to-infinitive relative is the more natural, formal choice

items.sentence: ___ you decide, let me know by Friday so I can book the venue.
items.why: whatever = any thing/decision, an open category

items.sentence: The exhibition, ___ opens next week, took two years to prepare.
items.why: non-defining relative clauses about things use which, never that

items.sentence: The storm damaged the roof, ___ meant the museum had to close for repairs.
items.why: which refers back to the whole previous clause

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one or two words.

items.sentence: The professor ___ office is next to the library has just published a new book.
The hostel introduced a rule ___ guests must leave their key at reception.
We interviewed fifteen witnesses, most ___ agreed on the sequence of events.
This is the very reason ___ which the trip was cancelled.
Liam was the first ___ notice the mistake in the timetable.
___ wins the scholarship will represent the school at the regional final.
The lecture overran by twenty minutes, ___ meant we missed the bus.
Take ___ route you prefer; both lead to the main square.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: This is the topic we disagreed about.
The manager is the person I sent my complaint to.
The school introduced a scheme so that students can borrow tablets for the term.
We tested fifty devices, and twelve of them failed within a week.
Mateo was the first student who solved the puzzle.
I don't mind which option you choose.

summary: Front the preposition before whom (people) or which (things) for a formal register: to whom, on which, by which.
Whereby and wherein replace preposition + which for systems, processes and legal or academic contexts.
After a quantity already mentioned, use number/quantifier + of which/whom, never which alone: ten of whom, none of which.
Whatever, whichever and whoever open the reference to any thing, option or person; only which — never that — refers back to a whole previous clause.
After the first/last/only and superlatives, a non-finite to-infinitive relative is often more natural than a finite clause: the first to arrive.
